lesson.title: Kalender I: Januar bis Mai
lesson.subtitle: five Latin month names, five German pronunciations

hook.title: Latin Names, German Mouths
hook.content: Every month in this lesson is a Latin month that never left. Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai — and the giveaway is German's stress: Januar, Februar and April carry it on the SECOND syllable — ja-NU-ar, fe-BRU-ar, a-PRIL — while one-syllable MÄRZ and Mai have nowhere else to put it. English tends to hold January on its first syllable, and when you learn German's months by ear you will be tempted to follow. Don't. And the grammar behind them is a one-off worth learning once: month names are masculine even though they end in -r, they take der (der Januar, not die Januare), and in dates they stand bare after the day — am 5. Mai, with no article in front of the name. One Monat has vier Wochen; a Jahr has zwölf Monate. The calendar is the one place where German and Latin never stopped talking.

footnotes.title: The March Surprise
footnotes.content: Der März is the month where German and English diverge least — but watch the stress: German MÄRZ, English March. The z is the same sharp sound you drilled in zehn and zwei. And April is nearly identical on both sides, which is a gift rather than a coincidence.

pattern.title: Saying the Date
pattern.content: Three frames, all of them old. 1. With a preposition: im Januar, im Februar, im März, im April, im Mai — 'im' is in + dem, and dem is the masculine, so the month name follows it bare. 2. As a subject: Der Januar ist kalt (January is cold). 3. In a date: am 5. Mai, am 1. April — the ordinal number, a dot, then the name with no article. And the arithmetic you already own: ein Monat hat vier Wochen; ein Jahr hat zwölf Monate.
pattern.linguist_note: The masculine gender of the months is a Latin leftover: Latin Ianuarius was a masculine proper name, and proper names kept their gender when they turned into common nouns. English lost the gender along with the names; German kept it, so you get der Januar and das Jahr — one Latin, one Germanic: das Jahr is the same old word as English year, native to the family, not a Latin guest.

exercises.prompt: The first five months — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: In February the children play in the garden
matching_pairs.german: Im Februar spielen die Kinder im Garten

exercises.target_answer: Der Januar ist kalt, Im Februar spielen die Kinder im Garten, Im März regnet es, Im April regnet es oft, Im Mai ist es warm
exercises.explanation: im = in + dem, so the masculine month name follows it bare. Every one of these five sentences is something a German will actually say about the weather.

exercises.prompt: '___ April regnet es oft.' (In April it often rains) — which preposition-plus-article contracts to im?
exercises.explanation: Month names are masculine, so in + dem = im. Compare am Montag (an dem) and im Garten (in dem) — same contraction law, different genders.

exercises.prompt: One month has at least how many full weeks?
exercises.explanation: vier — the same word you counted with two lessons ago. Ein Monat hat vier Wochen; ein Jahr hat zwölf Monate; and die Woche is a K→CH word, the ch of Milch and Buch.

exercises.prompt: Which of the five month names is nearly IDENTICAL in English and German — letter for letter?
exercises.meaning: April ↔ April: the same Latin name both languages kept whole
exercises.explanation: April survives untouched on both sides. Januar became January with an added J, and Februar and März kept their consonants while English rewrote their vowels.

vocab_hints.note: K→CH: die Woche carries the same ch as Milch and Buch. And the plural after a numeral is bare — vier Wochen, nicht vier die Wochen.

exercises.explanation: hat in slot 2, then the bare numeral and its bare plural. Swap Monat for Jahr and the same frame gives you the year.

summary.outcome: Name the first five months, use im + the bare name, and state the month-to-week arithmetic.

use_example.german: Im April regnet es oft — ein Monat hat vier Wochen.
use_example.english: In April it often rains — a month has four weeks.

summary.takeaway: Der Januar, der Februar, der März, der April, der Mai — masculine, bare after im, and always stressed on the first syllable.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Juni bis Oktober, the second half of the year's Latin wardrobe.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Kalender I: Januar bis Mai (A month has four weeks):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ein Monat hat vier Wochen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Kalender I: Januar bis Mai without relying on short-term echo.

januar.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Iānuārius. [wiktionary]

februar.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Februārius. [wiktionary]

märz.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin Martius via Middle High German merze. [wiktionary]

april.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Aprīlis. [wiktionary]

mai.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin (mensis) Maius via Middle High German meie. [wiktionary]

monat.etymology_derivation: The twin of English month, from *mānōþ 'moon' (see der Mond) — th→d included. [wiktionary]

jahr.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *jār — the twin of English year. [wiktionary]

woche.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Berlin.
woche.context_translation: Next week I travel to Berlin.

oft.context_translation: We often play in the park.
oft.etymology_derivation: Old High German ofta — the true twin of English oft/often. [wiktionary]

vier.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *feuwar — the direct twin of English four. [wiktionary]

garten.context_translation: The children play in the garden.

kinderzimmer.context_translation: The child plays in the children's room.
kinderzimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of Kind and Zimmer with linking er; Kind is cognate with English kin, and Zimmer with English timber. [wiktionary]

schaf.context_phrase: Das Schaf steht auf der Wiese.
schaf.context_translation: The sheep stands in the meadow.
schaf.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German schâf, from Old High German scāf, from Proto-Germanic *skapą. English sheep is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

überraschung.context_phrase: Das Geschenk war eine große Überraschung.
überraschung.context_translation: The gift was a big surprise.
überraschung.etymology_derivation: From überraschen, to come at someone too quickly — its rasch (quick) is cognate with English rash. [wiktionary]

fett.context_phrase: Diese Wurst ist zu fett für mich.
fett.context_translation: This sausage is too fatty for me.
fett.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *faitid; the page compares English fat — the same Germanic fat-word (German doublet: feist). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
